notes:
I found enough for notes on every verse. A few things are missing. I found no Lutheran, Pentecostal, Orthodox, bibleodyssey or netbible sources on this psalm. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on it. The enduringword page only came back as a short search preview, and the Blue Letter Bible copy of the same study guide (Guzik) loaded without its text. Points from pages I read in full (Gill, Augustine, Wesley) have the web address but no citation tag.

**Title ("A song of ascents")**
- One of the songs pilgrims used as they went up to Mount Zion. The Biblical Illustrator — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-121.html
- Gill lists older guesses about the setting: the Syriac title links it to the return from Babylon; Grotius thought David wrote it during Absalom's revolt; others call it a soldiers' or travellers' psalm. Gill thinks it fits any time. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-121.html

**v. 1**
- *Which hills?* The Pulpit Commentary says the holy hills around Jerusalem, where God had promised his blessing (Ps 133:3). Wesley says Zion and Moriah (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/121.htm). Barnes weighs three options: hills where help might come from, heaven, or Jerusalem's hills. He thinks Jerusalem most likely and calls the "heaven" reading forced. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/121-1.htm
- *Statement or question?* Ellicott says the King James wording, which reads like "the hills, from which my help comes", is wrong. It follows the old Greek and Latin translations. He says the question is not doubt; it is asked to set up the strong answer in v. 2. — https://biblehub.com/psalms/121-1.htm. Chuck Smith says the verse is often misquoted as if help came from the hills, when the hills can't help you; the line is a question. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/psalms/121-1.html
- *Looking past the hills:* Gill notes some read it as "shall I look to the hills?", meaning idols worshipped on hills, with the answer no. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/121-1.html. Matthew Henry makes the same kind of point: don't rely on men and means, or on princes; trust God only. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/121-1.htm
- Gill also calls lifting the eyes a prayer gesture that shows boldness and confidence in prayer. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/121-1.html
- Calvin thinks the opening speaks in the person of an unbelieving man. Read with v. 2, it means looking to the hills is a mistake until the eyes are fixed on God alone. — https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_5/psalm_121_1-2.htm
- Got Questions sees a pilgrim near Jerusalem looking toward where God lives, a declaration of trust and dependence upon God for help. — https://www.gotquestions.org/I-lift-my-eyes-to-the-hills.html

**v. 2**
- Gill: God helps his people in every need, and he is able to because he made heaven and earth. "What is it that he cannot do?" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-121.html
- Calvin: calling God the Creator here is meant to rebuke the ingratitude of men, when they cannot rest contented with his power. — https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_5/psalm_121_1-2.htm
- Constable: the psalmist reminds himself that his help is the God who had made those hills. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/121-1.html

**v. 3**
- *Promise or prayer?* Spurgeon says in the original the words express a wish or prayer. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps121.cfm. Precept Austin notes the Greek Old Testament reads "Let not thy foot be moved; and let not thy keeper slumber." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61168
- Pulpit Commentary: God does not sleep; his watch never stops (comp. Isa 27:3). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-121.html
- **Where traditions differ (can believers fall away?):**
 - *Gill (Calvinist Baptist):* the verse promises "final perseverance". Believers may come close to slipping but will never fall "finally and totally". — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-121.html
 - *Spurgeon (Baptist):* if he will not suffer it we shall not suffer it. Yet his devotional also turns the promise into prayer: keep me, lest I wander and fall and perish. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61168
 - *Wesley (Methodist):* his short notes say nothing on this verse (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/121.htm). I found no Wesleyan teacher arguing against the Calvinist reading here.
 - *Pulpit Commentary:* says God keeps us upright in righteousness if we have to walk "in slippery places". — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-121.html
- *Catholic (Augustine):* the foot slips through pride. That is how the devil fell, while love moves the feet upward. He reads the verse as a prayer that God answers. — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801121.htm

**v. 4**
- Gill: this points back to Jacob, whom God kept while he slept (Gen 28:15). God may seem asleep when help is slow, but he never is. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-121.html
- Calvin: the verse turns from one person to the whole church, to recall each individual to the consideration of the common covenant. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/121-4.html
- Calvin's note: heathen people believed their gods sometimes slept. — https://ccel.org/study/Psalms_121:0-121:0?comm=1
- Spurgeon: v. 3 is about one person, v. 4 the whole nation, so mercy to one saint is the pledge of blessing to them all. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61168
- Clarke (Methodist): God is pictured as a watchman, who takes care of the city through the night. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lsb/psalms/121-4.html
- *Catholic (Augustine):* "Christ keeps Israel". Israel means "seeing God", first by faith, later by sight. Every human guard dozes and dies, so don't trust in man. — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801121.htm

**v. 5**
- *Shade:* Pulpit Commentary: shade means protection, and the right hand mattered as the side which no shield guarded. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-121.html. Calvin's note: the Hebrew means "shadow", like a tree's shade or a sunshade, and is often put for defense in general. — https://ccel.org/study/Psalms_121:0-121:0?comm=1. Wesley: shade from the sun's heat (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/121.htm).
- Guzik: this recalls the cloud by day that followed Israel in the wilderness. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-121.cfm
- Gill reads the Keeper as Christ, the Word of God (he notes the Targum, an old Aramaic paraphrase, says "the Word of the Lord" in v. 7). He also links the pillar of cloud to Christ shielding us from God's wrath. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-121.html
- *Catholic (Augustine):* he reads the Latin "the hand of your right hand" as a hidden meaning. The left hand stands for things of this life, the right for eternal promises, and "the hand of your right hand" is faith, the power to become God's children (John 1:12). — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801121.htm

**v. 6**
- *Literal readings:* Wesley says the sun smites "with excessive heat" and the moon with night cold and damp, which cause disease (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/121.htm). Guzik notes the brutal rays of the sun on pilgrims. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-121.cfm
- *Broader readings:* Coffman says it means protection from the dangers of the day and of the night, not just sunstroke or being moonstruck. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/psalms-121.html. Gill says it is not strictly literal (Jacob and Jonah suffered sun and cold) but means persecution. He notes the Targum speaks of spirits that strike by day and night. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-121.html
- *Catholic (Augustine):* plainly figurative, since the moon doesn't burn. The "burning" is stumbling in faith: the sun stands for errors about God (such as the Arians on the Trinity), the moon for errors about the Church. — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801121.htm

**v. 7**
- *What "all evil" means:* Gill says not freedom from trouble but from sin's rule and final falling away, and from Satan's power. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-121.html. Precept Austin: no promise of no pain; we may be hurt but not harmed. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_121_a_commentary
- Spurgeon: "Soul keeping is the soul of keeping. If the soul be kept all is kept." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-121.html
- **Where traditions differ (does the promise depend on us?):** a writer quoted in Spurgeon's Treasury calls this an absolute promise, there are no conditions annexed. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-121.html. R. Tuck in the Pulpit Commentary says God's soul-keeping runs along with, and works through, our own soul-keeping. S. Conway adds that God may preserve a man's soul when he lets his outward affairs go all to ruin. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-121.html
- *Catholic (Augustine):* the soul, not the body, is kept. Martyrs lost their bodies but not their souls; his example is the martyr Crispina. — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801121.htm

**v. 8**
- *Background:* the Pulpit Commentary says the phrase comes from the blessing on obedience in Deuteronomy 28:6, and that "forevermore" rather implies that these will never cease. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-121.html
- Spurgeon: going to work and coming home, and also going out in youth and come in at the end to die. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps121.cfm. Precept Austin notes the Greek word for "going out" (*exodos*) can refer to the end of earthly life. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_121_a_commentary
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: going out and coming in mean the beginning and the completion of undertakings, and the repeated "preserve" shows how much our unbelief needs reassurance. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-121.html
- Gill: God guards and prospers all of life, in time and forever. The Targum reads it as going out to business and coming in to study the Law. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-121.html
- Perowne (via Spurgeon): keeping "thee, thy soul, thy going out and coming in" shows the protection covers all that the man is and that he does. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-121.html

**Modern scholarship (whole psalm)**
- Most later critics read v. 1b as a question (Pulpit Commentary, citing Cheyne): https://biblehub.com/psalms/121-1.htm
- Maclaren dates the Songs of Ascents to the times of the Exile. He pictures an exile in Babylon longing for hills he can't see. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/121-1.htm
